## Abstract

Recent efforts to improve the predictability of TALYS-2.0 calculated charged-particle residual product cross sections have focused on adjusting parameters related to the optical model potential and pre-equilibrium process. Although adjusted TALYS-2.0 outputs show marked improvements in agreement with experimental data over the default parameters, the procedure is generally time-consuming due to the need for sequential TALYS-2.0 calculations. Since the models and model parameters must be defined and constrained prior to adjustment, we show in this work that an artificial neural network can serve as a surrogate model to successfully predict TALYS-2.0 outputs within this domain of input parameters. No practical differences were observed in the trained model’s performance between uniform random, Latin hypercube and Sobol sequence sampling for generating the training datasets. Once validated, trained neural network models were used to adjust TALYS-2.0 nuclear model parameters, where a multi-parameter fitting procedure was not only feasible but optimal for this process. The neural network approach is >1000x faster at generating residual product cross sections than using TALYS-2.0 directly, and a high-fidelity surrogate model could be implemented with ~1500 TALYS-2.0 files to achieve adjusted cross sections comparable to the previous publication.

#### Keywords:

## 1 Introduction

Nuclear transmutations have been an invaluable basis for supplying critical isotopes used in fundamental research [1, 2], medical [3, 4] and security [5] applications. The availability of high-quality nuclear cross section data is therefore essential for optimizing the production of radioisotopes from various pathways. If experimental data does not exist, nuclear modeling codes serve as a predictive source for isotope production applications [3, 6]. These codes often have adjustable parameters that could be tuned to achieve better agreement with experimental data and future generalizability.

A comprehensive set of charged-particle nuclear cross sections for various target materials of interest to the U.S. Department of Energy Isotope Program were previously measured by the Tri-lab collaboration between Brookhaven National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and Los Alamos National Laboratory [7, 8, 9, 10]. During the evaluation of these measured cross sections, the authors implemented a parameter adjustment procedure using the TALYS-2.0 [6] nuclear reaction model code. However, this iterative workflow currently requires sequential TALYS-2.0 calculations, which makes the parameter adjustment process time-consuming and limits parallelization.

Alternatively, simpler models that approximate the complex function of interest, commonly referred to as surrogate models, are often implemented for computationally challenging tasks [11]. In building these models, a major advantage is that a small subset of the true model output can potentially represent the problem domain. Since surrogate models evaluate much faster than true models, the total computation time can be significantly reduced. Surrogate modeling has thus been considered in a variety of applications, such as data science, engineering and fundamental physics [12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. Furthermore, by leveraging recent technological advances in machine learning, surrogate modeling can become more generalizable and effective than simple analytical functions [17, 18, 19, 20, 21].

In this work, we demonstrate that the TALYS-2.0 parameter adjustment process can be facilitated by interpolating nuclear model parameters using an artificial neural network (NN) as a surrogate model (see Figure 1). TALYS-2.0 datasets were generated in parallel using either a High-Performance Computing (HPC) cluster at Brookhaven National Laboratory or a standalone Ryzen 7960X CPU. Initially, datasets with three variable parameters were used to characterize the performance of the NN model and enable comparisons with a conventional cubic interpolator. The three parameters chosen here are used in the semi-empirical expression for the squared matrix element, which is relevant to the pre-equilibrium process in TALYS-2.0 [6]. After evaluating the 3-parameter surrogate model, datasets with six variable parameters were used to test the feasibility of the NN model for scaling up to more practical scenarios. Finally, the NN model was evaluated on datasets varying seventeen parameters matching those previously published for proton-induced reactions on (effectively) La-139 [10]. After validating the performance of the NN model for generating cross sections based on different nuclear model parameters, trained NN models were used to adjust these parameters based on experimental data for 139La(p,x) nuclear reactions.

## 2 Surrogate modeling using artificial neural networks

### 2.1 TALYS-2.0 cross section dataset generation

The TALYS-2.0 nuclear reaction model code was used to generate residual product cross section datasets due to its ease of accessibility, suitability for proton induced reactions and ability to use a two-component exciton model for the pre-equilibrium process [10]. For all NN models in this work, the training dataset was uniform random sampled for splitting into training the NN model and for validating the model outputs at each epoch. Test datasets were only used for evaluating the trained model and separated from the training dataset. Proton-induced reactions on natCu were initially chosen to balance the available reaction pathways and TALYS-2.0 computation time. Energy sampling similar to TENDL [22] was chosen to reduce computation time while retaining sufficient data points to cover the range of interest. Details of the datasets for surrogate models investigated in this work can be found in Table 1.

### 2.2 Artificial neural network architecture and training methodology

Artificial NN models were implemented using PyTorch 2.5.1 [23] and Python 3.11 [24]. An Intel® Core™ i7-13700 CPU with 64 GB memory was used for establishing the NN model. A single fully connected deep feedforward NN was chosen to establish a working surrogate model for TALYS-2.0. The size of the NN was optimized based on the validation performance, training/computation time and memory constraints (final nodes in hidden layers: 256, 128, 512, 512 and 512). The NN model was trained using the AdamW optimizer [25, 26] with a Huber loss metric [27, 28]. The learning rate decayed after every 500 epochs, and training was stopped based on the validation performance. Overfitting was mitigated by incorporating weight decay, batch normalization and dropout. The activation function of the input, hidden and output layers were SELU[29], Mish [30] and ReLU [31, 32], respectively. Residual product cross sections were normalized by the maximum cross section of the respective reaction channel from the default TALYS-2.0 output for training the NN model.

### 2.3 Surrogate model evaluations

#### 2.3.1 3-parameter model

A total of 4096 files were generated via a 16x16x16 grid (16 values for each of the three nuclear parameters) to assess the performance of the 3-parameter surrogate model against a conventional cubic interpolator. The full training dataset (training and validation) for the NN model were provided as sample points for the multidimensional cubic interpolator, and both models were evaluated based on their performance for 30 residual products with the largest integrated cross sections from 0-200 MeV.

In a direct comparison using 9x9x9 training data (parameter values: 0.20, 0.31, 0.47, 0.72, 1.1, 1.7, 2.6, 4.0 and 5.0), the conventional cubic interpolator was able to achieve a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.11 mb and 5.3 mb maximum absolute error (MAE) for the test dataset. Similarly, the NN model achieved 0.24 mb RMSE and 4.7 mb MAE for the test dataset. However, in contrast to the conventional interpolator, the NN model was more robust when trained with a 6x6x6 dataset (parameter values: 0.20, 0.38, 0.72, 1.4, 2.6, 5.0), achieving 0.22 mb RMSE (0.89 mb interpolator) and 5.6 mb MAE (50 mb interpolator). This performance difference is illustrated in Figure 1, where both models trained with 6x6x6 TALYS-2.0 files were used to generate cross sections from the test dataset. These results suggest that the NN model can achieve good agreement with TALYS-2.0 generated cross sections for small training datasets.

*Figure 1: Comparison between the NN surrogate model (red solid) and standard cubic interpolator (red dotted) after training with 6x6x6 TALYS-2.0 files. The cubic interpolator incurred substantially larger errors than NN for generating the test data (red circle). For reference, the reaction channel shown is natCu(p,x)51Cr, and three separate parameter sets used for training both models are plotted as black hollow markers for illustration.*

#### 2.3.2 6-parameter model

With 6 nuclear model parameters and the increased test dataset size (~65k files), the conventional cubic interpolator was unable to compute ~66 million cross sections within a reasonable amount of time (>1 day). Alternatively, the NN model could predict the cross sections in <1 min and achieved 0.71 mb RMSE and 49 mb MAE with just 300 TALYS-2.0 files for the training dataset. The hyperparameters obtained from evaluating the 3-parameter NN model required only minor adjustments for optimization. However, likely due to the increased dimensionality and larger test dataset size, approximately twice as many training files were needed to achieve comparable RMSE to the 3-parameter NN model.

#### 2.3.3 17-parameter model

Continuing from promising results with the 6-parameter NN model, the surrogate modeling was expanded to interpolate 17 nuclear model parameters. These parameters and associated ranges were previously selected by Morrell et al. [10] to improve agreement between TALYS-2.0 outputs and experimental measurements for 139La(p,x). The reaction cross sections were calculated via TALYS-2.0 using the same model selections (ldmodel 5, strength 10, deuteronomp 2, alphaomp 4, preeqspin 3). Short-lived parents of residual products from reactions used in the parameter adjustment procedure were also included in the NN model. As such, this scenario serves to illustrate a realistic application of the TALYS-2.0 surrogate model approach for nuclear model parameter adjustments. Three different sampling methods (uniform random, Latin hypercube [33, 34, 35] and shuffled Sobol sequence [36, 37, 38]) were selected for the training dataset to assess potential differences in the performance of the trained NN model.

Based on RMSE, 99th percentile absolute error (P99) and MAE, NN models trained with different sampling methods were roughly comparable with the same number of training files (Figure 2, Figure 2 and Table 2). Larger training datasets generally achieved better performance and no observable differences in individual reaction channels were observed for the different sampling methods (Sobol: Figure 3, Latin hypercube: Figure 4, and uniform: Figure 5).

*Figure 2: Different metrics used to evaluate the performance of the surrogate model trained using files sampled from uniform (blue triangle), Latin hypercube (LHC, orange circle) or Sobol sequence (green square) sampling. All three sampling methods are generally comparable and show a general trend of improved performance with increasing training dataset size.*

To verify the robustness of the NN approach for other target material, natCu(p,x) nuclear reactions were assessed using the same set of nuclear model parameters, physics model selection, NN architecture/hyperparameters and training dataset size. A set of 26 reaction products were chosen to span cross sections from 0.1-500 mb. The NN model’s performance was also evaluated using a test dataset of 25k uniform random sampled files within the specified parameter bounds. Without any modifications to the hyperparameters, the NN model for natCu(p,x) achieved similar results to 139La(p,x) with similarly sized training datasets (Figure 6).

## 3 Parameter adjustment using the trained neural network

After validating the NN model’s ability to predict cross sections by interpolating outputs of different nuclear model parameters, the best performing NN model in this work (Sobol with 2048 files) was chosen to replicate the parameter adjustment procedure from [10]. Each parameter was optimized sequentially starting from “rvadjust n” to “Cstrip a” and repeated until convergence (i.e., a “1-D” adjustment procedure). Since the convergence criteria was not explicitly provided, this was set as 0.001 relative difference since the last full set of parameter iteration. The chi-squared figure of merit (FOM) was weighted by the average fractional contributions of the integral cross sections from 0-200 MeV and the maximum cross section of each reaction product based on default TALYS-2.0. Also, maintaining the same procedure as before, the weight for Ce-134 was increased by a factor of 2 due to its potential as a diagnostic congener for Ac-225 radiopharmaceuticals. The NN model was used to generate 100 datapoints for each parameter with (parameter scaled) linear spacing. The resulting best-fit parameters were then used in TALYS-2.0 calculations to verify the NN model. Experimental cross section data used for parameter adjustment were taken from [39, 40, 10, 41], where data with no reported uncertainties or uncertainties <5% were set to 5%.

The 1-D parameter adjustment procedure using the NN model achieved comparable results to [10] (Figure 7), and the NN generated cross sections mostly agree with TALYS-2.0 (Figure 8). However, despite the comparable residual product cross sections, several parameters were noticeably different from the previously determined set of parameters by [10] (Table 1). These discrepancies could be explained by the lack of sensitivity for several parameters (Figure 9) and slight differences in the convergence criteria and experimental uncertainty data. Several of the 1-D adjusted parameters are also at the ends of their respective ranges, which could contribute to greater deviations from the true TALYS-2.0 outputs since less training data are expected to exist at these extremes.

Alternatively, since the NN surrogate model effectively approximates TALYS-2.0, a multiparameter (“N-D”) adjustment procedure was also implemented to assess potential differences in the two procedures. For the N-D procedure, a dual annealing algorithm [42, 43, 44] was used to perform a constrained optimization for the parameters (iterated 10 times). In comparison to the 1-D procedure, the N-D procedure took about 8 min to complete (3 min for 1-D) but achieved better agreement with TALYS-2.0 (Figure 8) and slightly improved FOM (Figure 3).

## 4 Discussion

The primary aim of this work was to demonstrate that the nuclear model parameter adjustment procedure could be parallelized to benefit from manycore processors/HPC systems. Artificial NN were identified as potential surrogate models for TALYS-2.0 due to their good generalization for complex and high-dimensional tasks [45, 46, 47]. Training datasets for the NN models can be generated in parallel and even prior to experimental evaluations, but physics models and their associated parameters must be clearly identified. In this work, the optimal number of training files for adjusting 17 constrained parameters using a NN model was between 1024 to 2048 TALYS-2.0 output files. Using only a standard Intel i7-13700 CPU for training the NN model (no GPU boost) and an AMD Ryzen 7960X CPU for generating TALYS-2.0 files, a TALYS-2.0 surrogate model can be implemented in <24 h for 139La(p,x). Since both the dataset generation and NN training are parallelizable, access to modern HPC clusters and GPU(s), respectively, can further reduce the total processing time to a few hours, which would be 10-100x faster than the sequential parameter adjustment approach. Hyperparameters for the 17-parameter NN model were also robust for natCu(p,x), suggesting that this approach could be generalized for other target nuclei. Additionally, the corresponding lightweight surrogate models enable FOM sensitivity analysis and conventional global optimization techniques that would otherwise be impractical.

A (shuffled) Sobol sequence sampling was hypothesized to more effectively train the NN over uniform random and Latin hypercube sampling due to its favorable coverage of multi-dimensional space (Figure 10). Based on the metrics used in this work, Sobol sequence sampling was practically indistinguishable from the simple uniform random sampling method and requires sampling files according to a base power of 2. In a direct comparison, an NN model trained using 1536 uniform random sampled files could achieve similar results to one trained with 2048 files from Sobol sequence sampling (Figure 3 and Table 3). Similar results were also observed for 1536 Latin hypercube-sampled training files.

The parameter adjustment process resulted in an improved fit to the experimental data for all methods investigated in this work compared to default TALYS-2.0. Larger discrepancies between the NN model and TALYS-2.0 were observed for adjusting parameters with the 1-D approach compared to N-D. This behavior is likely due to the lack of training data near the extreme bounds of the parameter values, where the 1-D procedure is more likely to compound these extremes since the process does not vary parameters in multidimensional space. Even with a relatively strict convergence criteria for the N-D adjustment, the process converged in 8 min with over 100k parameter set evaluations which is >1000x faster than calculating cross sections using TALYS-2.0. Additionally, another major benefit of the surrogate model approach is that the parameter adjustment process itself, such as changing the experimental dataset/FOM and down selecting parameters/reaction channels, can be altered without recalculating TALYS-2.0 datasets. The resulting FOM from the N-D adjustment was also slightly better than both 1-D and Morrell et al. [10], though improvements to FOM were not the focus of this work.

Future work aims to further reduce the number of files needed to implement a high-fidelity TALYS-2.0 surrogate model, either by optimizing the NN architecture or through different machine learning techniques. The NN approach could also be expanded to incorporate several target nuclei for the same physical models and parameters, where a single multi-target nuclei model would likely require fewer training files than multiple standalone models. Although not explored in this work, an independent module to upscale the incident particle energies per reaction and excitation energy bins would also greatly reduce the computation time for all TALYS-2.0 related tasks.

## 5 Summary and conclusions

A TALYS-2.0 surrogate model was implemented by using artificial neural networks to generate residual product cross sections for at least 17 variable nuclear model parameters. High fidelity TALYS-2.0 surrogate models were established by training with ~1500 TALYS-2.0 output files and achieved >1000x speedup in computation time for generating nuclear cross sections. Hyperparameters used for training 139La(p,x) models were also validated for natCu(p,x), suggesting generalizability for other target nuclei. A multi-parameter dual (simulated) annealing optimization resulted in lower deviations between TALYS-2.0 and the surrogate model with improved fitting to experimental data. Future work aims to further reduce the number of training files needed to establish a TALYS-2.0 surrogate model and to expand the approach for a wider range of target nuclei.

# Nuclear Data Evaluation Utilizing Bayesian Monte Carlo Methods

Catherine E. Apgar,1, ∗Lee A. Bernstein,2, 3 Yun-Hsuan Lee,2 Wilson Lin,4 Alan B. McIntosh,5 Dmitri G. Medvedev,4 Jonathan T. Morrell,4 Ellen M. O’Brien,1 C. Etienne Vermeulen,1 and Andrew S. Voyles2

1Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, New Mexico 87544, USA 2Department of Nuclear Engineering, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, California 94720, USA 3Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California 94720, USA 4Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, New York 11973, USA 5Texas A&M University Cyclotron Institute, College Station, Texas 77843, USA (Dated: October 28, 2026)

While the body of experimental nuclear data continues to grow at a rapid pace, significant gaps persist. The lack of evaluated experimental data is far more pronounced in charged-particle reactions which are essential to a large portion of the isotope production community for vital medical, industrial, and national security interests. In the absence of experimental and evaluated data, isotope production relies on theoretical models that may result in low yield and isotopic impurities. This work investigates model and parameter adjustments in TALYS 2.0 to establish uncertainty bands on proton-induced cross sections, highlight influential parameters in calculations, and constrain adjustments within physically defensible bounds. The EXFOR dataset for proton-induced reactions on natural copper, comprised of 24 independent cross sections, was used for iterative Bayesian model updating. Upon convergence, parameters and their uncertainties were compared against 23 cumulative cross sections from EXFOR, highlighting the limitations of generalization. Various machine learning models were leveraged to predict TALYS performance, with a small neural network showing useful ranking capabilities across several generations, suggesting the use of a surrogate approach to screening for future evaluations.

## I. INTRODUCTION

The nuclear data pipeline is a rigorous, expensive and time-intensive process, from identification of nuclear data needs through to publication and application. Evaluated nuclear data libraries, such as ENDF/B-VIII.0 [1], are compiled using experimental measurements and extensive evaluation by subject matter experts in the nuclear data field. Despite these robust libraries’ data for neutron-induced reactions, evaluated data remain sparse for charged particle reactions of interest to the isotope production community. Many of these channels have not been sufficiently measured, necessitating the use of theoretical models for cross section predictions. The nuclear reaction modeling code, TALYS-2.0 [2], has been leveraged for this purpose, as seen in a steadily growing number of citations, and with the broad adoption of the TALYS-Evaluated Nuclear Data Library, TENDL-2023 [3]. TENDL provides evaluated cross sections using a combination of experimental nuclear data and randomized parameter variation established by the user to establish a goodness of fit through TASMAN-2.0[3]. The parameters in an individual theoretical calculation can be systematically varied on a per-keyword basis, or globally in TASMAN, to calculate a probability distribution based on the outputs from TALYS. The flexibility in TALYS’ over 400 tunable parameters provides users with options to explore variations to nuclear reaction models, and these

options grow exponentially when individual parameters can be further adjusted for each residual product. This establishes an optimization procedure using Bayesian Monte Carlo (BMC) methods to assign a weight for each set of TALYS input parameters and an optimized parameter set with an uncertainty band. This research explores alternatives to the current method by adjusting the random sampling window to a lognormal distribution around the default value utilizing Sobol sequencing[4] for optimal coverage within physically defensible boundaries as well as different methods for the χ2 goodness of fit to experimental data. With hundreds of knobs to fine-tune within TALYS, we focus on 85 parameters, similar to Alhassan et al.[5] to explore their predictive capabilities within TALYS when compared to experimental data. We explore various methods to establish a likelihood function and weighting factor for each iteration as well as normalization to reduce overfitting. This work additionally explores a proposal-posterior approach to develop a weighted ensemble and refine the iterative process. The results of the iterative process are calculated using individual residual cross section measurements and validated against cumulative residual cross sections to compare a holistic approach against a refined, individual residual product approach. While these results emphasize the continued need for a physics-informed evaluation, they also leave room for supplementary screening via neural networks to potentially down-select during the process to reduce compute and resources. The research proposed here is not intended to reproduce or improve on evaluated nuclear data efforts, but rather to explore alternatives and recognize their strengths and weaknesses.

## II. BACKGROUND

A variety of Bayesian Monte Carlo methods have been used in the evaluation of nuclear data and theoretical modeling of reactions[6–11]. This analysis establishes both predictions and their associated uncertainties for calculated cross sections, both for reactions that have been experimentally measured and for reactions for which sparse data exists. Experimental data is costly, from facility costs to analysis, publication, and evaluation. It is therefore imperative to have more robust theoretical models. The majority of evaluation effort has historically focused on neutron-induced reactions and benchmark evaluations with sparse data for charged particle reactions valuable for the isotope production community[12]. Evaluated charged particle reaction datasets are sparse, necessitating the use of theoretical models. The isotope production community relies on these models to inform production routes. TALYS, and the associated evaluated nuclear data library TENDL, have been leveraged for over 20 years to predict cross section measurements, and consequently, theoretical yields. TENDL is a trusted source for theoretical calculations and has been developed using an iterative Monte Carlo method through TASMAN and related T6 software[2]. This is a successful interpretation of neutron-induced reactions, but is focused on neutron-induced experimental data. Sparse datasets necessitate theoretical models, as well as associated uncertainties. One approach is the use of a Unified Monte Carlo method, which has been used for over a decade for analysis.[13, 14] The approach in this paper seeks to better quantify correlations not only among parameter adjustments in TALYS, but also among residual product results. The experimental dataset for this analysis uses proton-induced reactions on natural copper (natCu(p,x)) residual product production, as this is currently the largest dataset in the experimental nuclear data library, EXFOR, with over 2600 independent cross section residual product data points. We verify against the cumulative residual product cross sections from proton-induced reactions on natCu. In a broader overview, a target nucleus, bombarded by a proton, can produce hundreds of residual products with enough incident particle energy. While these cross sections are characterized, potential contaminants, including stable, long-lived, or otherwise unmeasurable residual products are important to characterize, motivating the use of theoretical models.

## C. Prior Sampling and Bayesian Updating

1. Generation of a Prior Distribution

An initial pass of 3000 TALYS calculations was generated to define the prior distribution over both discrete models and continuous parameters, allowing for a broad exploration of the physics-based models and tunable model constants. Discrete models were chosen at random, while continuous parameters were sampled using Sobol sequences with scipy.stats.qmc.Sobol [20, 21] to improve coverage over the high-dimensional parameter space, reducing clustering in comparison to simple random draws. Scrambling was enabled to add randomness while preserving the low-discrepancy properties[22]. These were drawn from a truncated lognormal distribution centered on the default TALYS parameter values for each parameter and sampled in log space with parameters µ=0 and σ=0.5. Here, µ=0 centers the distribution around the TALYS default parameter value and σ=0.5 creates a moderate spread around that default. Truncation

was enforced to ensure that the parameter values would not fall outside the allowed values within TALYS. This establishes a prior distribution as follows in Equation 1,2 for continuous parameters and Equation 3 for discrete parameters, with the overall prior distribution being a product of these.

For discrete model parameters, interpolation is not meaningful, so the value of these were fixed after the initial generation based on the best-performing sample, defined by the sample with greatest posterior weight.

Again, since these parameters function as multipliers, they were sampled using truncated lognormal distributions and Sobol sampling to sample efficiently. These subsequent generations of parameter sets were passed to TALYS, with the resulting theoretical cross section results again compared with experimental data to arrive at χ2 values and posterior weights.

5. Criteria for Convergence

This cycle of resampling was repeated iteratively, with successive generations fine-tuning the mean and uncertainty associated with the TALYS parameter set. This is done to reduce the uncertainty predicted in NDS-2022 and, not arriving at any specific set of parameter values for an optimized TALYS calculation, but instead to establish an uncertainty band in the predicted cross sections and parameters. Although each individual run will experience some measure of variation, convergence can be improved through large sample sizes and multiple generations. With this approach, it was determined that generations of 1000 TALYS calculations sufficiently covered the exploration space. Convergence was based on a number of criteria. The first criterion was a decreasing return on investment per generation based on the best χ2 value. Convergence could be considered when improvement over the current and prior generation was < 5%. Another criterion was based on the median χ2 value, when the reduction was < 10%. The effective sample size, or ESS, defined in Equation 16 provided guidance as well. This metric is useful to determine the number of samples that are actually having a significant difference on calculating the posterior distribution. The metric used here required at

## V. CONCLUSIONS

The work presented in this paper presents a systematic, iterative Bayesian Monte Carlo effort to establish uncertainty bands for nuclear reaction cross sections and parameters in the TALYS 2.0 nuclear reaction modeling code for natCu(p,x) reactions. The iterative sampling utilized 24 independent residual product cross section measurements from EXFOR. Substantial improvement was achieved from an initial, uninformed ensemble of TALYS model and parameter variations after five iterative generations. A reduction in the median χ2 was observed to decrease by 71.7%. This demonstrates this iterative process was successful in adjusting the default value and uncertainties of continuous parameters in TALYS. Each successive generation, while reducing effective sample size, maintained significant coverage. This suggests that the proposal distributions, truncated lognormal kernel density estimations, informed by the weighted posterior, were effective in reducing uncertainty distribution of parameter values. This was backed up by maintaining sufficient experimental data coverage within 1-σ uncertainty bands of the posterior distribution. Of note is the very small improvement in the best χ2

over generations, suggesting that the initial sampling of 3000 Sobol-sampled inputs had already explored the near

optimal set of model/parameter combinations. This is not surprising, but it is not the purpose of this work, and subsequent generations served to refine parameters and reduce uncertainty. This further suggests a well-defined prior distribution, with a truncated lognormal distribution around physically motivated default TALYS values. Further work, with significantly greater compute, could explore many more model combinations in the initial prior. This work does not suggest that the model combination chosen is perfect, but rather the best observed with available computational resources. The use of held-out cumulative cross section experimental data served as a check on the results, but this check indicated that the improvements did not transfer to these other reactions, despite the same incident particle and target material. This illustrates the limitations from a holistic approach and highlights the need for physics-informed evaluations in parameter adjustments for uncertainty reduction in theoretical nuclear models. A subsequent investigation into utilization of a surrogate model showed that while a simple neural network cannot accurately predict χ2 values and automatically iterate across generations, it can perform reasonably well in ranking input performance, suggesting the opportunity for a hybrid approach of surrogate-assisted down-selection and screening for the inputs likely to perform better than others. Overall, while not intended as a replacement for evaluated nuclear data, this work presents an exploration of iterative Bayesian strategies that highlight both the strengths and weaknesses of purely theoretical charged-particle reaction modeling.
